title: Work and power
question: What are work and power?

principle.name: Work and power
principle.formula: W = F × d · P = W ÷ t
principle.formulaNote: work = force × distance moved along the force, in joules; power = work ÷ time, in watts. One joule is 1 newton pushed through 1 metre, and one watt is one joule every second
principle.idea: You do work when a force moves something along the direction it pushes: work = force × distance, measured in joules. Power is how fast you do that work, work ÷ time, measured in watts.
principle.discovered: 1829 · Gaspard-Gustave Coriolis names force × distance 'travail' (work); power was already measured in horsepower by James Watt, 1783

examples.title: Running up the stairs
examples.text: A 60 kg student climbing one floor, 3 m, in 5 s does about 1,770 J of work at about 350 W. Few people can keep that up for more than a minute.

examples.title: Cycling to school
examples.text: Riding at 20 km/h on the flat takes about 80 W at the pedals, mostly to push the air aside. Most riders can hold 100 to 250 W for an hour.

examples.title: Low gears on a hill
examples.text: A bicycle's low gear works like a lever: each pedal stroke pushes less hard but you turn the pedals more times. The work to climb the hill stays the same.

examples.title: Engine horsepower
examples.text: A 1.2 litre hatchback makes about 90 hp, some 67 kW, and a 2.0 litre engine about 110 kW. Yet a petrol engine turns only about 30% of its fuel's energy into work.

examples.title: Brakes do negative work
examples.text: A 1,200 kg car at 100 km/h carries about 460 kJ of kinetic energy. Hard braking removes all of it in about 56 m and turns it into heat in the brake discs.

examples.title: A one-horsepower mixer
examples.text: A 750 W mixer grinder is almost exactly 1 hp, the power James Watt measured for a mill horse in 1782.

examples.title: Motorcycle power
examples.text: A 100 cc commuter motorcycle makes about 5.9 kW, about 8 hp, and a 150 cc sports commuter about 10 kW. That power is force × speed at the rear tyre.

examples.title: Fan hours add up
examples.text: A 75 W ceiling fan running 12 hours a day uses about 27 units a month; a 30 W BLDC fan doing the same job uses about 11.

examples.title: The geyser's 2 kW
examples.text: A geyser heats with a 2,000 W element, so half an hour a day uses 1 kWh, about 30 units a month: as much as a fan running 13 hours a day.

examples.title: You run at 97 watts
examples.text: 2,000 kcal of food a day is 8.4 MJ, about 2.3 kWh. Spread over 24 hours that is about 97 W, the power of an old light bulb.

hook: Pull a crate at an angle, wind a bucket up a well, and watch the joules pile up under a graph. Race up the stairs at 350 watts, meet Watt's horse, lift a rice sack with a lever, pulley and ramp, read your electricity bill in kilowatt-hours, and find out why holding still makes you tired but does no work.

explainer.title: Force times distance
explainer.text: You do work when a force moves something along its direction: W = F × d, in joules. Pull at an angle and only F cos θ counts. On a force–distance graph, the work is the area under the line. If nothing moves, no work is done.

explainer.title: Power is a rate
explainer.text: Power is work ÷ time, in watts. Running up 3 m of stairs in 5 s, a 60 kg student makes about 350 W. A cyclist holds 100 to 250 W. Watt's mill horse did 33,000 foot-pounds a minute: 1 hp = 745.7 W.

explainer.title: Machines trade force for distance
explainer.text: Levers, pulleys, ramps and gears let a small force do a big job, but only by moving further. Work in = work out, minus friction. A bike chain is about 97% efficient; a petrol engine about 30%.

explainer.title: Paying for work
explainer.text: Electricity is sold by the kilowatt-hour: 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ. A 1.5 kW AC for 6 hours a day uses 270 units a month. Food is energy too: 2,000 kcal a day is 8.4 MJ, an average of about 97 W.

explainer.title: Myths and limits
explainer.text: Carrying a bag level does no work on it: the force is at 90° to the motion. More power doesn't mean more work, just faster work. Brakes do negative work. And holding still tires you because myosin heads keep burning ATP without moving anything.

concepts.def: Energy handed over by a force that moves something: force × distance moved along the force.
The unit of work and energy: a force of 1 newton acting over 1 metre.
How fast work is done: work ÷ time, or force × speed.
The unit of power: one joule every second.
James Watt's unit of power: 33,000 foot-pounds per minute, 745.7 W.
1,000 W for one hour: 3.6 MJ. One 'unit' on an electricity bill.
How many times a machine multiplies your force. It always costs the same factor in distance.
Useful work out ÷ energy in. The rest is lost, mostly as heat.
